recent_posts.title: React.Children.only expected to receive a single React element child
recent_posts.summary: React.Children.only error occurs when a React component expects a single child element but receives multiple or invalid elements. This can happen when passing arrays directly as children or making incorrect conditional renderings. To fix this, always map arrays to React elements and wrap them in a container. Ensure to wrap multiple elements in one and check the conditional rendering syntax. Common components that use Children.only internally include Modals, Portals, Tooltips, Context providers, and Animation wrappers.

recent_posts.title: One-Way vs Two-Way Door Decisions: A Framework for Better Choices
recent_posts.summary: The post introduces a mental model to help with decision-making by categorizing them as one-way or two-way door decisions. One-way door decisions are final and hard to reverse, like major rebranding or tech shifts. Two-way door decisions can be reversed easily, such as small design tweaks. Jeff Bezos popularized this at Amazon, and the framework is used at Figma for determining the decision type and applying the appropriate process. This model helps teams avoid overthinking reversible decisions while ensuring irreversible ones are carefully considered.

It's a straightforward approach that doesn't require special training, encouraging curiosity and thorough problem investigation.

recent_posts.title: Vercel AI SDK reference notes
recent_posts.summary: Vercel AI SDK is a free, open-source JavaScript library that offers a unified interface for working with various Large Language Model (LLM) providers. It simplifies the integration of different AI models in both frontend and backend environments, without needing to use Vercel's hosting services. The SDK includes core components for backend, frontend UI, and React Server Components, along with features like text and object generation, model switching, message history management, and processing images and PDFs.

recent_posts.title: Principles for building great AI Interfaces
recent_posts.summary: Traditional software interfaces are evolving from static visual elements to dynamic, AI-driven processes. Voice interfaces like Vapy highlight the importance of low latency for natural interactions. Gum Loop uses visual workflows to manage AI agents, improving oversight and modification. Grid interfaces turn open-ended prompts into structured data, and adaptive interfaces like Zuni change options based on context. AI is driving a shift from fixed elements to active processes in software design, significantly impacting user experience.

recent_posts.title: Agent Recipes (code & visuals)
recent_posts.summary: Sequential processing involves executing LLM operations in a predefined sequence where each step's output serves as input for the next. Routing dynamically sorts input for specific handling based on its characteristics. Parallelization allows multiple operations to run simultaneously, combining their results. The orchestrator-worker pattern uses a main LLM to plan tasks and assigns them to specialized worker LLMs. The evaluator-optimizer pattern refines outputs through iterative feedback loops until they meet quality standards. Lastly, multi-step tool usage involves LLMs using tools repeatedly to solve problems, ensuring structured outputs by using a specific 'answer tool' to finalize the process.

recent_posts.title: AI as a Judge: Practical Implementation Guide
recent_posts.summary: AI can be used to automatically evaluate and improve the outputs of other AI models, ensuring higher quality and safer responses. Practical implementation includes patterns like the evaluator-optimizer pattern, comparative evaluation, and simple quality threshold checks. Cost optimization strategies include using smaller models, sampling, self-evaluation for simple checks, and discrete scoring. Best practices involve defining clear criteria, using examples, and tracking consistency over time.

recent_posts.title: AI Model Design for dummies
recent_posts.summary: When designing AI models, key decisions such as architecture choice, model size, and context length are crucial. Transformer architecture enables the model to process entire sentences and prioritize important words, while model size affects speed and cost. The context length determines how much information the model can retain at once. Understanding these basics helps in selecting the right AI model for different tasks and recognizing their limitations.
